Oakvale Food Cooperative — A Community-Owned Grocery
Welcome! This page is for anyone thinking about shopping with us as a member. Below you will find how our cooperative works and the simple steps to join.
How our co-op works
Oakvale is owned by the people who shop here. Since we opened in 2009, our members have shared in the decisions that shape the store, from the products we stock to the local farms we partner with. Members are not employees; they are neighbors who help guide the store and buy their weekly groceries here. Today more than 1,200 households hold a membership. Two years ago, members funded a new solar roof, which now supplies part of our electricity. All members also receive a monthly newsletter and reduced prices on cooking workshops.
A shared goal this year
This year we are working to open a fresh bakery counter at the back of the store. Building it is a demanding project that cannot be finished by staff alone. It will require both contributions from members and hours of volunteer help. We expect the counter to open before the end of the year, offering bread baked on site each morning.
Becoming a member
Joining is easy. First, complete a short form at the customer service desk. Second, pay a one-time equity share of $25, which is refunded if you ever decide to leave. Third, attend a brief orientation so you understand how the store runs. There is no monthly charge, and your share makes you a part-owner right away.
Store hours: Monday to Saturday, 8:00 A.M. to 8:00 P.M. Questions? Speak with any staff member or stop by the service desk. We look forward to welcoming you.

Workshop Spotlight
Cut, Stitch, Repeat
By Rebecca Lyle
A quiet studio in Braxton is teaching newcomers to make their own leather goods entirely by hand.
On a side street in Braxton, behind the wide windows of Thornbury Leather Studio, a row of visitors bend over their workbenches, pressing needles through strips of tan leather. None of them had made anything from leather before this month, and that is exactly the point. This spring the studio began offering a set of hands-on workshops built for complete beginners, and the seats have been filling quickly.
The program is arranged in three levels. First Stitch, the entry point, is a single two-hour session that requires no experience and sends participants home with a finished card holder. Everyday Carry runs across two evenings and guides makers through cutting, dyeing, and assembling a folded wallet. The longest option, Satchel Studio, fills a full weekend and ends with a completed shoulder bag. Tools and materials are provided at every level.
Every class is led in person by Julian Reyes, who opened the studio after spending three years apprenticing with a saddlemaker in Florence. "I was taught slowly, by hand, and that is how I teach here," Reyes said. "People are surprised by how much they can finish in one sitting once someone shows them where to place the needle."
Classes run on weekday evenings and weekends, and places can be reserved through the studio's website. Reyes recommends First Stitch as a starting point for anyone unsure whether the craft suits them.
